title: Why Bitter Coffee Starts to Taste Better
summary:
Your first sip of black coffee can taste awful. Our brains are wired to avoid bitterness, yet millions of people grow to love that taste. Scientists at UC San Francisco may have found part of the answer.

The team studied dopamine, a chemical messenger for motivation, reward and learning. This study, published November 4 in Nature, looks at a slow dopamine system that responds to news from inside the body.

When food reaches the gut, sensors spot nutrients such as sugar and fat, and the brain can answer with a dopamine response that builds slowly and lasts several minutes.

Knight and Grove gave mice sugar water or a milkshake-like liquid straight into their stomachs. The strongest response showed up in the anterior basolateral amygdala, or BLA, a brain area for emotion and learning.

Blocking the pathway left mice eating normally, but they could no longer learn that a new flavor meant calories were coming. When the team switched the fibers on, mice learned to like a flavor with no calories. Once the brain links coffee's taste with caffeine's lift, Knight said, coffee tastes a lot better.
why_it_matters: It helps explain why foods you once disliked can start to taste good after you try them a few times, just like a new food at school lunch.
